711675.t: Borrowed from Semitic, the same source of Latin simila (“wheat flour”), Arabic سَمِيذ (samīḏ), Aramaic סְמִידָא / ܣܡܻܝܕܳܐ (səmīḏā), from Akkadian 𒆠𒅔𒆠𒅔𒄯𒄯 (/⁠samīdu⁠/, “a type of fine groats, coarse flour, semolina”), related to Akkadian 𒀀𒊏𒄯𒄯 (/⁠samādu⁠/,…

711632.t: From σείω (seíō, “to shake”) + -μός (-mós). The "earthquake" sense is an ellipsis of γῆς σεισμός (gês seismós, “shaking of the earth”).

711609.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tségʷomai, from Proto-Indo-European *tyegʷ- (“avoid, yield to”).

711625.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tseřřā́, from Proto-Indo-European *twer-yeh₂- (“seizing”), from *twerH- (“to grab, seize, enclose”).

711682.t: From the radical of σέβομαι (sébomai) + -νός (-nós), with regressive assimilation.

711631.t: From σείω (seíō, “I shake”) and the suffix -μα (-ma).

711651.t: Clearly related to σέλμα (sélmă, “deck of a ship”). These words have been compared to Old English selma and syll, and to German Schwelle (“threshold”), but phonetically this etymology is unconvincing.
